edits.old: Consideration is a bargained-for performance or return promise (Restatement (Second) § 71), and courts do not weigh its adequacy. They imply good-faith or reasonable-efforts duties to keep promises from being illusory, and count a surrendered claim that was doubtful or honestly believed (§ 74).
edits.new: Consideration is the performance or promise sought in exchange. It need not benefit the promisor or be an equal economic trade. An implied duty can make an apparently optional promise binding; surrendering a disputed claim can also count. The cases apply different jurisdictions’ rules, and the Restatement organizes those rules without enacting them.

edits.old: The Restatement § 90 formulation requires a promise, expected and actual reliance, and injustice avoidable only by enforcement; relief may be limited as justice requires. These state cases show different applications and limits, including at-will expectations and Texas’s writing requirement. Cosby concerns a separate due-process route.
edits.new: Under the Restatement § 90 approach, a promise can bind when reliance was expected, actually occurred, and enforcement is necessary to avoid injustice. The remedy may be limited. State adoption and other requirements still matter: reliance does not automatically create a final contract, guarantee expected profits, or satisfy a writing requirement.

edits.old: Assent is judged objectively, by what a reasonable person in the other party's position would understand from words and conduct. An advertisement is usually an invitation, but one that is definite and leaves nothing to negotiate is an offer. Acceptance is an outward commitment to the offered terms, made in the manner the offer invites; unless the offer clearly says otherwise, any reasonable manner will do (UCC § 2-206, Restatement (Second) § 30). An acceptance by performance generally needs notice when the offeror would not otherwise learn of it.
edits.new: Assent depends on outward words and conduct in context. An offer invites commitment; acceptance makes that commitment in an allowed manner. Goods offers generally permit any reasonable method unless the offer clearly indicates otherwise. Whether performance needs separate notice depends on the offer and whether the offeror would learn of it.

edits.old: When civil actions in different districts share common questions of fact, the Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation may transfer them to one district for coordinated or consolidated pretrial proceedings if that serves convenience and the just and efficient conduct of the actions (§ 1407(a)). The transferee court manages pretrial work (Rule 16.1) and decides federal questions under its own circuit's law, but it cannot keep a case for trial: each action must be remanded unless it has ended (Lexecon), though a party may waive remand if the waiver is clear and unambiguous. Centralization is pretrial coordination, not merger: it does not make anyone a party to another action, and a settlement class built inside an MDL must still satisfy Rule 23 (Amchem).
edits.new: Section 1407 permits coordinated pretrial work when common factual questions and efficiency justify it. It ordinarily keeps the actions separate and requires unresolved transferred cases to return for trial; Lexecon bars self-assignment, while clear waiver is a separate issue. Rule 16.1 structures initial management. Neither centralization nor settlement removes Rule 23’s class-certification requirements.

edits.new: Delegation means giving another official power to carry out a statute. Follow three different jobs: finding a fact that activates Congress’s rule, filling in details, and choosing policy within statutory limits. An “intelligible principle” is Congress’s guidance for that choice. A plurality is a rationale joined by fewer than a majority; Benzene and Gundy need that distinction.
